name: Recency effect
statement: The last items in a list are recalled best, and in immediate free recall thirty seconds of filled delay removes that advantage.
meaning: Ask someone to recall a list in any order and plot accuracy against the position each word held. The curve bows up at both ends. The rise at the end is the recency effect, and the smaller rise at the start is primacy. Recency is the larger of the two in immediate free recall, and it is the part that a filled delay destroys. That fragility is why the effect was read for decades as a readout from a short-term store holding the last few items. The reading is now disputed, because recency returns when a distractor task is placed between every item as well as after the last one. Two separate claims travel under the one name. The first is this memory finding, which holds in almost every participant tested. The second is a claim about judgement, that raters, auditors and investors weight recent information too heavily, and it rests on a thinner and more mixed literature.

origin.note: Murdock's paper is the one the field cites for the free-recall serial position curve, but the curve was already in the literature: Glanzer and Cunitz's reference list carries Deese and Kaufman's 1957 serial-effects paper and Raffel on primacy from 1936. The mechanism paper is Glanzer and Cunitz in 1966, which separated the two ends of the curve by manipulating each independently.

evidence: Glanzer and Cunitz ran the two experiments that made the curve into an argument. In the first, 240 Army enlisted men heard eight 20-word lists at one word every 3, 6 or 9 seconds. Slower presentation raised recall across the first fifteen positions and did nothing to the last five. Summing correct responses in blocks of five gave F of 23.46, 16.21 and 22.00 for the first three blocks, all p < .001 on 2 and 235 degrees of freedom. For the last block F was 1.71, p > .10. In the second, 46 enlisted men saw fifteen 15-word lists and were then shown either a cross-hatch, meaning write, or a digit, meaning count aloud from that number until told to write. Ten seconds of counting removed most of the end peak and thirty seconds left no trace of it. Delay was significant only in the last five positions, F(1,45) = 22.42, p < .001, against F = 3.60, p > .05, for the first five and F = 1.44, p > .10, for the second five. A pilot using thirty seconds of empty delay with no task did cut the end peak, F(1,233) = 37.00, p < .001, but a clear end peak survived, which is why the counting task was added. A footnote records Postman and Phillips reporting similar results in 1965. Their abstract, deposited at Crossref, reports lists of 10, 20 and 30 words read at a word a second. Recall was tested after 0, 15 or 30 seconds of counting, and the loss fell mainly on the terminal items while the early positions held steady. Bjork and Whitten then broke the explanation. Twenty paid undergraduates at Michigan studied four lists of ten word pairs, with 12 seconds of arithmetic before and after every pair and 20 seconds after the last one. Both primacy and recency appeared anyway. Forty more undergraduates saw four kinds of list. On lists with no interpolated arithmetic, adding 30 seconds of arithmetic before recall flattened recency, as Glanzer and Cunitz had found. On lists with 12 seconds of arithmetic around every pair, the same 30 seconds did nothing to the recency portion of the curve. A word in the latter lists waited seven times as long for recall as its counterpart in an immediate list, and recall was about the same at every position except the last few.

examples.tag: The list called out from the kitchen
examples.text: Someone reads nine items down the hall and the shopper gets to the door with the last three and nothing from the middle. Primacy leaves the first item or two as well, and the tail is the larger of the two bulges.

examples.tag: The directions and the phone call
examples.text: A stranger gives five turns and the last two are still there at the corner. Take a call for half a minute on the way and the tail advantage is gone, which is why the effect was read for years as a small store being emptied.

examples.tag: The eight introductions at a reception
examples.text: Someone is walked round a circle of eight and, released at the end, can produce the last two names and the first one. The six in the middle went past at the same speed and with the same attention.

replication.headline: Healey and Kahana gave 126 people 112 lists each and found that 90% of them showed recency individually, not merely in the group average.
replication.detail: The concern with a curve of this kind is that averaging hides people who did something else. Healey and Kahana tested it on the Penn Electrophysiology of Encoding and Retrieval Study, 126 participants aged 17 to 30, each studying 112 lists of 16 words for immediate free recall. Defining recency as higher mean recall across the final six positions than across positions 5 to 10, 90% of participants showed it on both no-task and task lists. Defining primacy as higher recall for items 1 to 4 than for mid-list positions, 93% showed that. Recall started at the final item for 64% of participants on no-task lists and 79% on task lists, and average initiation probability for mid-list items was under 1%. The task manipulation there is a size or animacy judgement made during study, not a distractor before recall, so every list was an immediate test. Those judgements are the depth-of-processing manipulation of entry no. 216, used here only to vary study conditions. What has not survived intact is the explanation. Thapar and Greene report that substantial recency remained when a different distractor task followed every list position, which they read as evidence against the short-term store. Their five experiments were aimed at the claim that long-term recency needs practice at the distractor task, and practice made the task easier without restoring the buffer account. Davelaar and colleagues argue the opposite way from the same literature: short-term and long-term recency have different properties, and two components are needed, an episodic contextual system plus an activation-based buffer. So the effect replicates and the mechanism is open.

study.cite: Healey, M. K., & Kahana, M. J. (2014). Is memory search governed by universal principles or idiosyncratic strategies? Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 143(2), 575-596.

limits: Nothing above is an effect size, and none of the memory papers reports one. The memory literature here quantifies recency as recall probability by position and as the proportion of people showing the pattern, so the structured effect-size fields are empty rather than filled with a number no source contains. The applied claim is the weaker half of this entry by a wide margin. Hogarth and Einhorn's belief-adjustment model rests on five experiments and 192 adults, and the ERIC record says only that order effects arise from the interaction of processing strategies and task characteristics. The paper itself stayed shut on 21 September 2026, so nothing is claimed here about what the model predicts. Steiner and Rain manipulated where a single good or poor performance fell among average ones. Study 1 used 333 undergraduates watching four videotaped lectures in one session. Its deposited abstract breaks off mid-sentence after reporting a recency effect for overall ratings, so nothing further from it is quoted. Trotman and Wright reviewed the auditing literature on order effects in 2000 and their own summary is that the results are mixed and stayed mixed after two more studies. On the finance side, Greenwood and Shleifer regressed six survey measures of expected stock returns on the past twelve months of returns and the price level. Panel A of their table 3 runs each survey twice, once against the log price and once against the log price-dividend ratio, and the average R-squared of 0.40 is taken across all twelve of those regressions rather than across six. In the log-price columns the coefficient on past returns was positive and significant for four of the six surveys. It was not significant for the Graham-Harvey series, t = 1.377, and it was negative and not significant for the Shiller series, minus 1.878 at t = minus 0.205. Graham-Harvey turns significant in the price-dividend columns, at t = 2.460, so the count of four belongs to one specification and not to the paper as a whole. Those figures come from the NBER working paper, the only version open on 21 September 2026, and the published article may renumber its tables. Murdock's 1962 paper was not obtained. APA answers an Incapsula bot challenge rather than a paywall, and Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive and the Wayback Machine held no copy on 21 September 2026. What appears above about it comes from the sentence Glanzer and Cunitz devote to its presentation-rate conditions and from a truncated abstract record. Thapar and Greene was read in full this time, from the publisher's own PDF. Davelaar and colleagues was read from the abstract the publisher deposited at OpenAlex. Searches on 21 September 2026 ran at Crossref, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, ERIC and general web search, and OpenAlex refused search queries that day on a rate limit. None returned a meta-analysis of the serial position effect.
misreadings: The commonest error is the textbook one. Most pages that explain recency say it is items still sitting in short-term memory, and offer the thirty-second distractor as proof. That manipulation works only in the immediate paradigm. Put a distractor between every item as well as at the end and recency comes back, which is what Bjork and Whitten found and what Thapar and Greene confirmed against the obvious objection. The short-term store may still be part of the answer, and Davelaar and colleagues argue it is, but a page that presents the buffer as settled is a page that stopped reading in 1968. The rival account runs on context and retrieval cues, the argument entry no. 253 covers. The second error is transfer. The memory effect is close to universal, at 90% of individuals in the Penn sample, and the judgement claim called recency bias in management and investing writing is a different assertion with its own much weaker record. Auditing researchers who tested it directly describe their own results as mixed. Robustness in one does not carry to the other. The third error is treating recency as the whole curve. Primacy appeared in 93% of the same participants, and in Glanzer and Cunitz the two ends respond to opposite manipulations: slower presentation lifts the start and leaves the end alone, filled delay flattens the end and leaves the start alone. The last error is scale. Healey and Kahana put it as a ratio: recency depends on the gap between successive items relative to the gap between the last item and recall. So recency is not a fixed span of items, and it survives long delays when the spacing is stretched to match.
